newsitem.title: USA: Tear gas, bullets as Florida city erupts in race riots.
newsitem.headline: Tear gas, bullets as Florida city erupts in race riots.

text.p: Police used tear gas early on Thursday to disperse small groups of angry youths firing guns and throwing rocks after a grand jury refused to bring criminal charges against a white police officer who killed a black motorist last month.

At least five people were injured in the sporadic outbreak of fires, shooting and rock-throwing that began on Wednesday evening in a predominantly poor, black neighbourhood where more widespread violence first erupted on Oct. 24.
One police officer was shot in the leg and another officer in a helicopter was grazed by a bullet. Three civilians were also injured, according to local television reports.

Much of the violence broke out near the headquarters of a black activist group, the National People's Democratic Uhuru Movement. The group, already under investigation by federal prosecutors for its role in last month's riot in the city, advocates using violence to create a separate black society.
The Uhuru group, named after the Swahili word for "freedom," recently called for the execution of St. Petersburg's police chief and mayor after conducting its own trial.

"We've had threats, constant threats for the past two weeks, saying that if the report from the grand jury didn't meet with their satisfaction that the town was going to burn," Police Chief Darrel Stephens told reporters at a late night news conference.

City officials said the Uhuru group showed little signs of willingness to help negotiate a solution to the complaints of many black citizens, who claim they have been victimised by police, the lack of jobs and bleak prospects for years.
"They are so radical, so far out of a reasonable range. I like to work with all groups but I'm afraid that may not be possible with this group," St. Petersburg Mayor David Fischer said.
More than 225 police officers in riot gear cordoned off the area to try to control bands of youths who ran through the streets throwing bottles, firing weapons and setting fires.

Officer Keith Glasgow, 39, was shot in the leg after police responded to a report of gunfire in the neighbourhood that was rocked by rioting last month, St. Petersburg police spokesman Bill Doniel said.
Joe Lassen, the co-pilot of a Pinellas County sheriff's helicopter, said one bullet pierced the glass canopy of the aircraft, passed through his shirt sleeve and grazed his arm.

Police stepped up patrols after a grand jury ruled on Wednesday afternoon that Officer James Knight was justified in the fatal shooting of motorist Tyron Lewis, 18, following a routine traffic stop three weeks ago.

The shooting was followed by hours of rioting in south St. Petersburg. At least 11 people were hurt, mostly police officers, and nearly 30 fires were set in shops, businesses and homes before police regained control of the streets.
State prosecutors said the 16-member grand jury had determined the death of Tyron Lewis "was the result of a justifiable homicide under Florida law." The panel included one black member.
Following the grand jury ruling, the police department suspended Knight for 60 days without pay for violating its firearms policy.

But the grand jury ruled the death of Lewis was justifiable homicide because Knight was in danger of being run over by the car Lewis was driving after he and his partner, Sandra Minor, pulled Lewis over for speeding.

Knight, 34, appeared before the grand jury on Tuesday to provide his account. He has been on administrative leave since the shooting. Minor, one of the first witnesses to testify in the case, also testified on Tuesday.
